title: DFS on San Francisco: Real Streets Traversal ⚡
description: Watch Depth-First Search (DFS) dive through Mission District intersections like a stack-driven explorer—going deep before it backtracks. This reel visualizes graph traversal mechanics you can use for real routing problems and LeetCode graph theory.
ig_caption:
Depth First Search (DFS) Traversal on Real Street Maps… what happens when DFS explores city intersections ⚡

In this visualization, each street intersection is a node and each connecting street segment is an edge—turning Mission District into a graph. DFS uses a LIFO stack (or recursion) to keep going down the current branch until it can’t, then it backtracks—so you’ll see a “deep dive” path instead of a shortest-path route.

🧠 How it works (technical but visual):
- Mark a node as visited to prevent cycles
- Push neighbors (ordering matters!)
- Recurse/iterate depth-first until dead-end
- Backtrack to the most recent branching point

✅ Takeaway: DFS is great for exploring structure (connectivity, reachability, component discovery) but it does NOT guarantee the shortest path—BFS is the usual comparison.

Debate question: If you reorder neighbor directions, should the “DFS street path” be considered a different answer—or just a different traversal trace?
